Reader report submitted to Blurry Report: Blythe, Georgia. About 6:00 a.m. on January 1, 2025.

Phil was driving northeast on Highway 1 beside a pecan orchard, doing about 65 mph on his way to work just as the sun was coming up. Out the right side of his windshield, he noticed a light above the trees, maybe 100 feet off the ground.

It kept pace with his truck for about 10 to 15 seconds. Then, just as he started to really get a look at it, it shot off to the northeast at extreme speed and disappeared at the horizon. It moved so fast it created a visual effect, like the light stretched out long ways in the direction it went.

From the moment it zipped away to the moment it vanished at the horizon, Phil says it was less than a second. In his words, it "looked faster than anything flying around the Augusta, GA area."

Seen something strange yourself? Submit your report at blurryreport.com and it could be featured here.

Answer: C) Montauk Monster

The Montauk Monster washed up at Ditch Plains beach near Montauk, New York, in July 2008. Jenna Hewitt and three friends said they found the strange hairless carcass on July 12, and on July 23 the local paper The Independent ran her photo under the headline "The Hound of Bonacville." Guesses ran from a turtle without its shell to an experiment from the nearby Plum Island Animal Disease Center. Gawker posted it on July 29, and the photo went everywhere. Nobody ever produced the body. Hewitt said a guy took it and put it in the woods in his backyard. Stony Brook University's William Wise called it a fake, or maybe a diseased dog or coyote, but paleozoologist Darren Naish studied the teeth, skull and front paws and concluded it was a raccoon, made strange by decomposition and the sea. Jeff Corwin agreed.

How'd you do?

Jackson, Tennessee. About 8:05 p.m. on October 13, 2026.

A man in Jackson steps out to his vehicle in the driveway and, as usual, glances up at the clear night sky. This time he does a slow double-take. What he sees looks like an unfamiliar constellation: three oddly placed bright stars giving off a soft white light, like Venus, arranged in a triangle.

Then he wonders if they are moving. They are, very, very slowly, all in unison, drifting from north-northeast to south-southwest. Then he notices a satellite moving in the opposite direction. He knows that one is a satellite, so what are these?

As he watches, the triangle seems to spread out wider, and the three lights gradually fade away, seeming to pick up speed ever so slightly as they go. The whole thing lasts somewhere between 30 seconds and a minute. There is no sound at all. And of course his phone is not with him. He had actually reached for it at first, hoping to identify the constellation with a stargazing app.

He is honest about what it might have been. In his report to UFOIndex, he says it very well could have been satellites, and that night vision can be tricky. But he is content with calling them UFOs, and he adds, "even if they were satellites, it was a sight to see." He hasn't heard any other reports, and thinks maybe one other person saw it too.

Source: https://www.ufoindex.com/report?report=2430

Edmore, Michigan. October 1890.

James O. Scotford, a sign painter from Edmore, says he has dug up something incredible near Wyman in Montcalm County: a clay cup covered in strange symbols, and carved tablets. Soon looters are digging all over the area, and a syndicate forms to sell what comes out of the ground.

In 1907 Scotford teams up with Daniel E. Soper, a former Michigan secretary of state who had resigned amid accusations of embezzlement. Together they present thousands of objects said to come from 16 counties: coins, pipes, boxes, figurines and cuneiform tablets showing biblical scenes, including Moses handing out the Ten Commandments. On November 14, 1907, the Detroit News reports they are selling copper crowns from the heads of prehistoric kings and copies of Noah's diary. Father James Savage, a Detroit priest, buys 40 of them and believes until his death in 1927 that they were made by descendants of the Lost Tribes of Israel.

Scholars had already called it. In 1891 a professor dismissed the finds as "humbugs of the first water." Experts noticed the cuneiform was stamped in random order, the lions had no tails, the clay had dried on a machine-sawed board, and some objects fell apart in water. In 1911 Scotford's stepdaughter signed an affidavit saying she had seen him making them. Neither man ever confessed.

Savage's collection eventually passed to Notre Dame and then to the LDS Church. Testing in 2001 found marks of contemporary tools, and in 2003 the LDS Church gave 797 of the objects to the Michigan History Museum in Lansing, where a display was titled "Digging Up Controversy."

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_relics

Independence, Missouri. Haunted season, fall 2026.

In a shop on the Historic Independence Square, a small cat figurine falls to the floor. Then, by the owner's account, it rolls back and forth on its own, about four times. "This is probably the creepiest thing that's happened that kind of shook me," Sherri Corwin of Mixed Wildflower and Co. told KSHB 41. She also describes a door opening by itself, a picture flying over her head and curtains moving, and she blames it all on an owl statue in the store named Oliver.

Her shop is one of 13 stops on Paranormal Pursuit, a free digital passport from Visit Independence that runs from September 23 through November 6. Visitors check in at each reportedly haunted location to unlock prizes like an embroidered patch, a heat-activated mug and a long-sleeve tee. "Once the veil closes," the bureau warns, "so does your chance to complete the pursuit."

The headliner is the Vaile Mansion, a 31-room home built in 1881 for Harvey and Sophia Vaile. Sophia died in the house in February 1883 while Harvey was away in Washington, D.C. She had been diagnosed with stomach cancer and was found dead of a morphine overdose, a suspected suicide. Visitors and volunteers have reported unexplained experiences there, and the best known legend is a woman some believe is Sophia, seen near the windows or on the grand staircase.

The other stops carry their own stories. At the Bingham-Waggoner Estate, people report a man's voice or a cough in empty rooms, and Harry Waggoner, who died in 1976, was a heavy smoker. At the 1859 Jail, where Frank James was once held and Jackson County Sheriff Henry Bugler was murdered in 1866, people tell stories of unexplained voices and apparitions.

Is any of it real? The bureau openly hopes the passport brings in new visitors and tourism dollars. Corwin, for her part, says she doesn't feel scared. "That's when I started talking to Oliver," she said. "I'm like, 'Hey, what's going on there?'"

Source: https://deadofnightdispatch.com/dispatches/independence-missouri-paranormal-pursuit-passport/

Wrightsville Beach, North Carolina. Around 9:45 p.m. on October 2, 2026.

A group of skywatchers is out at Wrightsville Beach, just east of Wilmington, with North Carolina UFO author Chris Bledsoe. In his words, "the sky, the ocean, and the tree line all came alive." He says multiple orbs were witnessed by the group, some moving high in the sky, others appearing over the water, and several rising up out of the forest behind them. "People were filled with excitement some were crying some filmed, and stood in quiet awe as the lights appeared from different directions at the same time," he wrote.

Bledsoe shared a video of the night on X on October 12, closing with a promise: "More nights like this are coming."

Skeptics on the Metabunk forum went straight to work. One member ran the Sitrec sky simulator for that location around 9:45 p.m. and found that Starlink satellite flares would have been visible right between the two houses seen in the video. Others pointed out what look like airplanes off to the sides and people on the beach shining lasers up at the orbs. Sky lanterns were floated and mostly ruled out, because two of the orbs cross paths, and lanterns drift together with the wind.

There is no exact time stamp for the clip, so even the skeptics admit a perfect match is hard to prove, though they say there is little doubt. Bledsoe and the group say they saw orbs. This one is disputed.

Source: https://www.metabunk.org/threads/multiple-orbs-seen-by-bledsoe-and-orb-watchers.15129/

Sonora, California. A Thursday evening in October 2026.

When the Stanislaus National Forest announced a Bigfoot presentation at its headquarters in Sonora, the post drew 112,000 views. Ranger Kathy Bowen Marquez says people called from Idaho, Oregon, Sacramento and the Bay Area. Reservations were capped at 75, and on the night more than 125 people packed the room, with more than 50 of them standing along the back and sides. A local Scout troop came, and some folks drove up from as far as Fresno.

Marquez shared Me-Wuk names for a giant of the mountain woods, including Yayali, the hairy giant. Then, in a video shown to the crowd, Forest Archeologist Kathy Strain told the story of Pinnacle Point Cave, where people trapped inside threw lit pine cones into the basket on Yayali's back until he burned and fell. His bones, the story goes, are the white marble out by Columbia Airport. Strain says Tuolumne County has the second highest number of Bigfoot sightings in California, and she pointed searchers to Pinecrest, Herring Creek and anywhere along Highway 108. "We had just a sighting not at all that long ago, just above Strawberry," she said.

When Marquez asked who believed, nearly every hand in the room went up. Fresno resident Ron Quitoriano, a member of the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization, described finding a line of bare footprints on a remote trail near Shaver Lake in 1995. In 2018, riding a dirt bike near North Fork, he heard a roar and saw something peeking out of the bushes about 100 yards up the hill. "I got that feeling that I shouldn't be here," he said. "So I skedaddled."

The forest says it can't confirm or deny that Bigfoot exists, and Strain reminded everyone that there are bears out there too. Staff say they will find a bigger room next time.

Source: https://www.uniondemocrat.com/news/article_810fd2c7-b21f-4c37-a2a9-d021fee9866c.html

St. Louis, Missouri. The Lemp Mansion, 3322 DeMenil Place, built in 1890.

Before Prohibition, the Lemp family ran one of the great breweries in America. William J. Lemp built his father's Western Brewery into the largest brewery in St. Louis, installed the first refrigeration machine in an American brewery in 1878, and made the Lemp name a dominant force in American beer, best known for Falstaff. The family's grand house stood in the Benton Park neighborhood.

Then the tragedies began. In 1901 Frederick, the son William had hoped would take over, died of heart failure. William grew despondent, and on February 13, 1904, he took his own life. His son Billy ran the brewery until Prohibition shut it down, and the plant was sold for $588,000. On December 29, 1922, Billy shot himself in his office. In 1949 his brother Charles, the last of the family to live in the house, shot himself in his bed and left a note that read, "In case I am found dead blame it on no one but me." The mansion is known for those three suicides. Edwin, the last surviving brother, ordered his art collection and family heirlooms destroyed before his death in 1970.

There is a debate inside the legend too. Their sister Elsa died of a gunshot in 1920 at her own home on Hortense Place. It was ruled a suicide, but some suspect it was a murder made to look like one, and a feature film exploring that idea has been in development.

After 1950 the mansion became a boarding house, and today it is a restaurant and inn that is reported to be haunted by the spirits of the Lemp family. The team from Ghost Hunters investigated it in 2010. Guests still book rooms for the night in the house where so much of the family ended. Whether the Lemps are still there is up to you.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemp_Mansion

Villisca, Iowa. The night of June 9 to June 10, 1912.

On a Sunday evening, Josiah and Sarah Moore and their four children walk home from the Presbyterian church's Children's Day program, which Sarah helped coordinate. Two young sisters, Ina and Lena Stillinger, come along to spend the night. The next morning, a neighbor notices that nobody has come out to do the chores. Josiah's brother unlocks the door and finds all eight dead, killed with an axe that belonged to Josiah himself.

The details still unsettle people. Two cigarettes left in the attic suggest the killer waited up there for the family to fall asleep. A gas lamp upstairs had its glass chimney removed and its wick turned down low. Every mirror in the house had been covered with cloth or clothing, and a slab of bacon had been taken out of the icebox and laid beside the axe. Within minutes of the alarm, townspeople crowded into the house, handling evidence and ruining the scene before the National Guard sealed it off.

That is where the controversy begins, because more than a century later no one has ever been convicted. Reverend George Kelly, a traveling minister who left town on a 5:19 a.m. train hours before the bodies were found, signed a confession in 1917, then took it back. His first trial ended in a hung jury, and a second jury acquitted him. A detective accused Frank Jones, Josiah's former employer and business rival, of hiring a man named William Mansfield, but payroll records placed Mansfield in Illinois and a grand jury declined to indict him. In 2017, authors Bill James and Rachel McCarthy James pointed to a drifter named Paul Mueller, tying the case to a string of similar axe murders.

The house was restored in the 1990s, and today the Villisca Axe Murder House is billed as one of the most haunted houses in the world. Ghost hunters book tours and overnight stays hoping to catch something from that night, and the house has been featured on Ghost Adventures, The Dead Files, Destination Fear, and BuzzFeed Unsolved. Whether anything lingers there is still debated. Who swung the axe is still a mystery.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villisca_axe_murders
posts.headline: Villisca, Iowa. The night of June 9 to June 10, 1912.

Have you heard of the Mercy Brown vampire incident?

Top 5 things to know about New England's real vampire panic:

1) In Exeter, Rhode Island, tuberculosis, then called consumption, tore through the family of George and Mary Brown in the 1880s and 1890s, and friends and neighbors came to believe something undead was behind it.

2) Mary died first in December 1883, followed by her eldest daughter Mary Olive in 1884, and in 1891 daughter Mercy Lena Brown and only son Edwin both fell ill.

3) Believing one of the dead was draining the living, villagers, a local doctor, and a newspaper reporter exhumed the bodies on March 17, 1892; Mercy's body showed normal decomposition, but the blood still found in her heart and liver was taken as a sign.

4) As the superstition demanded, Mercy's heart and liver were burned, the ashes were mixed with water into a tonic, and it was given to Edwin, but he died two months later.

5) Scholars have suggested the case inspired Lucy Westenra in Bram Stoker's Dracula, it is referenced in H. P. Lovecraft's The Shunned House, and George Brown, who never caught the disease, lived until 1922.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercy_Brown_vampire_incident

Have you heard of the Spear of Destiny?

Top 5 things to know about the lance said to have pierced Jesus:

1) In Vienna, Austria, an iron spearhead bound with a gold sleeve is kept among the imperial treasures of the Hofburg palace, one of several relics claimed to be the Holy Lance, also called the Spear of Longinus or the Spear of Destiny.

2) Only the Gospel of John mentions it: a Roman soldier pierced Jesus' side on the cross, "and immediately there came out blood and water," and later tradition gave that soldier the name Longinus.

3) Relics said to be the lance were being shown in Jerusalem by the 6th century, and by the Late Middle Ages spearheads and fragments claiming to be it turned up all over Europe, with major ones still kept today in Rome, Vienna, and Vagharshapat, Armenia.

4) Some were treated as a guarantee of victory: German king Henry the Fowler's lance was credited for winning the Battle of Riade, and in 1098 a crusader named Peter Bartholomew said a vision led him to a lance buried at Antioch, which many crusaders credited for their victory there.

5) Science has been less kind: researchers in Vienna dated the Hofburg spearhead to around the 8th or early 9th century and ruled out the 1st century, even though the gold sleeve added around 1354 calls it the lance and nail of the Lord.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Lance

Have you heard of the Tic Tac UFO?

Top 5 things to know about the Navy's most famous UFO encounter:

1) On November 14, 2004, Navy pilots training with the USS Nimitz carrier group about 100 miles southwest of San Diego, California, were sent to check out radar contacts that the cruiser USS Princeton had reportedly been tracking for about two weeks.

2) According to Commander David Fravor, the contacts would appear at 80,000 feet, drop rapidly toward the sea, then stop and hover at about 20,000 feet.

3) Fravor said he saw a white oval object about 40 feet long hovering above a disturbance in the ocean, and when he spiraled down toward it, it rose to mirror his jet and then vanished; four aviators in two jets say they watched it for about five minutes.

4) A later flight recorded an object on an infrared camera, and Lieutenant Commander Chad Underwood, who captured the footage, gave it the nickname "Tic Tac," partly inspired by a joke in the comedy Airplane!

5) The New York Times published the video in December 2017, and the Pentagon formally released it with two other Navy videos on April 27, 2020, but explanations still range from drones and camera artifacts to parallax and human error.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon_UFO_videos

Answer: A) Gloucester Sea Serpent

The Gloucester sea serpent was reported off Gloucester, Massachusetts, and the Cape Ann coast. The earliest alleged sighting near Cape Ann was recorded in 1638 by John Josselyn, but the heyday came in August 1817, when fishermen reported a serpent-like creature about sixty feet long with a head like a turtle and humps along its back. When the crew of the schooner Caravan fired a cannon at it, it vanished beneath the water. Reports piled up through 1819, and with a committee of the Linnaean Society of New England investigating, it became one of the best documented sea serpents on record. Some witnesses described a spear sticking out of its head, which led skeptic Joe Nickell to suggest a narwhal, and in 2023 Karl Brandt proposed harpooned sperm whales dragging overturned rowboats.

How'd you do?

Cedar Bluff, Virginia. About 10:00 p.m. on October 6, 2026.

A husband and wife are standing in their backyard near the Cedar Bluff and Richlands area of southwest Virginia when they notice a bright white light in the sky. At first it looks like a star. Then, as they watch, it seems to start moving.

Shortly after that, smaller white lights begin appearing from different directions. The couple estimate fifteen to twenty in all. They move irregularly and at different speeds, and they all seem to be heading toward a common point, where they appear to come together with the first star-like light. Then that first light moves off and eventually disappears.

The sky is clear and there is no sound. The lights seem to be over or beyond a hill, roughly to the northwest, with no buildings or towers in view. The couple also spot ordinary satellites that night, and they say these lights behaved differently. They watch for about thirty minutes, and it is still going on when they finally go inside.

It was not the first time. The couple say they saw essentially the same thing two nights earlier, in about the same part of the sky, for about the same length of time. Their report to the National UFO Reporting Center was posted on October 13 with no explanation attached.

Source: https://nuforc.org/sighting/?id=201459

Lake City, Minnesota. September 29, 2026.

If something really is swimming in Lake Pepin, Goran Pesic wants to pay sixty thousand dollars to the person who proves it. At an evening presentation at the Lake City Public Library, the local author and educator raised the reward for verifiable evidence of Pepie, the legendary monster of Lake Pepin on the Mississippi River, and launched his new book, The Greatest Mysteries of Lake Pepin.

The new bounty replaces a fifty thousand dollar reward set by the late Captain Larry Nielson, former skipper of the Pearl of the Lake paddlewheeler, who died earlier this year. Pesic says he will pay it out of his own pocket.

The stories go back a long way. Pesic says the legend has roots in Dakota belief. He points to an 1871 report in which two witnesses said they saw a monster the size of a rhinoceros or an elephant, and to the spring of 1897, when two rafters from St. Louis said they saw something at least twenty feet long in Lake Pepin.

Claiming the money will not be easy. The evidence has to come from the stretch between Bay City and Nelson, Wisconsin, and Wabasha, Minnesota. You need unedited high-definition photos or video with a local landmark like Maiden Rock bluff or the Lake City marina in the same frame, plus a biological sample that does not match native wildlife. A panel of marine biologists has to rule out a lake sturgeon, an alligator gar, a swimming deer, a log, or a hoax, and forensic experts have to rule out AI or editing. "My idea is always that people did see something," Pesic told KTTC. "So now, is that necessarily a monster or is it something that can be explained?" No new sighting came with the bounty, and as of September 30, no one had claimed it.

Source: https://deadofnightdispatch.com/dispatches/pepie-lake-pepin-monster-60000-bounty-goran-pesic/

posts.text:
Los Lunas, New Mexico. Hidden Mountain, first recorded in 1933.

About thirty-five miles south of Albuquerque, on the side of Hidden Mountain near Los Lunas, sits a boulder weighing more than eighty tons. Carved into a flat panel on its face is a nine-line inscription that some say is an abridged version of the Ten Commandments, written in an ancient Hebrew script. It is also known as the Mystery Stone or Commandment Rock.

The first recorded mention comes in 1933, when University of New Mexico archaeologist Frank Hibben is taken to see it. He later says the letters were covered with lichen and patina and barely visible, and that his guide claimed to have seen the stone as a boy back in the 1880s. Hibben believed it was ancient. Scholar Cyrus Gordon went further and proposed it was a Samaritan mezuzah carved sometime in the Byzantine period. If that were true, Semitic travelers reached the American Southwest long before Columbus.

Most archaeologists say no. The old Hebrew script was known to scholars by at least 1870, so a modern carver could have copied it. Critics point to grammar mistakes and to letter forms mixed from two different alphabets. Archaeologist Kenneth Feder calls it almost certainly a fake, noting there is no campsite, no trash, no trail of everyday objects that ancient visitors would have left behind. Hibben's word is clouded too, since he was later accused of fabricating data in other work.

Because of its weight, the stone has never been moved to a museum. Years of visitors scrubbing it to make the letters stand out have wiped away the natural patina that might have helped date it, and in April 2006 vandals obliterated the first line. Today you need a state land permit to hike up and see it.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Lunas_Decalogue_Stone
posts.headline: Los Lunas, New Mexico. Hidden Mountain, first recorded in 1933.

Sister Lakes, near Dowagiac, Michigan. June 1964.

In the summer of 1964, residents around Dewey Lake and Sister Lakes in southwest Michigan start reporting something big in the woods. They describe a creature covered in hair, about ten feet tall and around five hundred pounds, with glowing eyes. By June the story has national attention.

Police search the area of the sightings and find nothing. That does not slow anyone down. Thrill seekers and monster hunters pour into the little lake community all summer. Local businesses sell monster getaway gas, monster burgers, and monster hunting kits that come with a net, a flashlight, a squirt gun, a mallet, and a stake. Chicago newspapers start calling Sister Lakes Monster Town USA.

Not everyone is buying it. Several zoologists suggest people saw a bear, or maybe a gorilla. Cass County Sheriff Robert Dool and conservation officer William Rowe dismiss the monster talk, and within about a week the South Bend Tribune reports that nobody seems frightened anymore. In a 1983 look back, the same paper suggests the monster was dreamed up by intoxicated strawberry pickers.

The creature never fully went away, though. The 2016 Dewey Lake Boat Parade celebrated the legend, and Sister Lakes Brewing named a beer after the Dewey Lake Monster. It is also known as the Sister Lakes Sasquatch.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Lake_Monster

Celo, North Carolina. Before dawn on September 29, 2026.

A man in Celo, a small valley community in Yancey County, is called outside by his wife, who has spotted lights in the sky to the east, out over Celo Knob in the Black Mountains. The two of them stand and watch. There are five orange lights. Three of them hold a wide triangle that seems to rotate both sideways and up and down at once, like a gyroscope, while the other two move around the main three.

The lights fade out for roughly a minute at a time, then brighten again to an orange glow he says looks larger than a star. There are no flashing red or green lights like an airplane would show. The couple watch for about thirty minutes, and he records part of it on his phone.

He files a report, and the clip ends up on Reddit, where commenters say it is Starlink, a string of satellites catching sunlight one after another low in the eastern sky. A SpaceX Starship test flight had released Starlink test satellites about eighteen hours earlier. UAP Globe ran the numbers and found the whole case comes down to a timestamp. At 3:00 a.m., the time on his report, satellites at that height would sit in Earth's shadow and could not flare at all. At 4:17 a.m., the time a commenter says is in the video's metadata, the explanation fits almost perfectly. Neither time can be confirmed, so the case is still listed as disputed. The witness took the satellite answer graciously, thanked the commenter, and asked a couple of good follow-up questions.

Source: https://uapglobe.com/cases/celo-nc-2026

Have you heard of Robert the Doll?

Top 5 things to know about Key West's haunted doll:

1) Robert is a reportedly haunted doll in a sailor suit, said to have been made by Germany's Steiff company and bought by the grandfather of Key West artist Robert Eugene Otto on a 1904 trip to Germany, then given to young Otto as a birthday gift.

2) The doll stayed in the Otto family home at 534 Eaton Street, and in 1994 it was donated to the East Martello Museum in Key West, where it became a popular tourist attraction.

3) Legend says Robert can move, change his facial expressions, and giggle, and some stories claim he moved voodoo figurines around the room and was aware of what went on around him.

4) Local folklore blames him for car accidents, broken bones, job loss, and divorce, and museum visitors who fail to respect Robert supposedly suffer post-visit misfortunes.

5) He first left Key West in May 2008 for a paranormal convention in Clearwater, was featured in the first episode of Travel Channel's Deadly Possessions in 2016, and inspired a horror film franchise that began in 2015.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_(doll)

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Lost Colony of Roanoke?

Top 5 things to know about America's original disappearing act:

1) In 1587 about 115 English colonists led by John White landed on Roanoke Island, in present-day Dare County, North Carolina, on Sir Walter Raleigh's behalf.

2) On August 18, 1587, White's daughter Eleanor Dare gave birth to Virginia Dare, later celebrated as the first English child born on what would become US soil.

3) White went back to England for supplies, but the Anglo-Spanish War delayed his return until 1590, when he found the settlement fortified but abandoned, the houses dismantled, and his own buried trunks dug up and looted.

4) "CRO" was carved into a tree and "CROATOAN" into a palisade post, and since the colonists had agreed to leave a secret token for their destination, White was certain they had moved peacefully to Croatoan Island, but rough seas and a lost anchor forced him home before he could look.

5) Theories range from assimilation with Native tribes to massacre, and digs at a spot called Site X in Bertie County have turned up Tudor pottery and weapons, yet no conclusive answer has ever been found.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roanoke_Colony
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Lost Colony of Roanoke?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Bloody Mary?

Top 5 things to know about the ghost in the mirror:

1) Bloody Mary is a legend of a ghost, phantom, witch, or spirit conjured to reveal the future, said to appear in a mirror when her name is chanted repeatedly, and most sightings come from group play.

2) The older version was a divination ritual: young women walked backward up a flight of stairs in a dark house holding a candle and a hand mirror, hoping to glimpse their future husband's face, with the risk of seeing a skull or the Grim Reaper instead.

3) The modern ritual began to come together in the late 1960s, usually chanted into a mirror in a dim or candlelit room or a bathroom, three times or, in some stories, forty-seven times.

4) She may appear as a corpse, witch, or ghost, sometimes covered in blood, and the lore warns she may scream, curse, strangle, or scratch your eyes out; some versions call her Hell Mary or Mary Worth.

5) Proposed real Marys include Mary I of England, who had around 300 Protestant dissenters burned at the stake, and Japan's modern Hanako-san legend strongly parallels the whole idea.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloody_Mary_(folklore)
posts.headline: Have you heard of Bloody Mary?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Majestic 12?

Top 5 things to know about the UFO world's most famous secret committee:

1) Majestic 12, or MJ-12, is a purported secret committee of scientists, military leaders, and government officials supposedly formed in 1947 by an executive order from President Harry S. Truman to recover and investigate alien spacecraft.

2) The earliest known reference to "MJ Twelve" is a 1981 document used in a disinformation campaign against UFO researcher Paul Bennewitz, who believed craft from US airbases were linked to cattle mutilations.

3) On December 11, 1984, Jaime Shandera, who was working with UFO author Bill Moore, received an anonymous package with a New Mexico postmark holding an undeveloped roll of 35 mm film.

4) The film showed a "Top Secret" Truman memo dated September 24, 1947, and a "Top Secret/Eyes Only" briefing for President-Elect Eisenhower, but the FBI later called the documents "completely bogus," and starting in 1989 people involved confessed to fabricating MJ-12 lore.

5) Despite its roots in deception and forgery, the name lives on in UFO conspiracy circles and in television, film, video games, and books.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majestic_12
posts.headline: Have you heard of Majestic 12?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Ark of the Covenant?

Top 5 things to know about the Bible's most sacred chest:

1) The Ark was a chest of acacia, or shittim, wood gilded with gold, about two and a half cubits long, with an ornamental lid called the Seat of Mercy and two cherubim on its cover, where God is said to have spoken with Moses.

2) According to Exodus it held the Tablets of the Law given to Moses at Mount Sinai, and other books add Aaron's rod and a pot of manna.

3) When priests carried it into the Jordan, the river is said to have run dry as soon as their feet touched the water, and the Ark was carried around Jericho for seven days before the city's wall fell down flat.

4) When the Philistines captured it, their idol Dagon was found fallen prostrate before it and then broken, and tumors and a plague of rodents followed it from Ashdod to Gath and Ekron until they sent it back after seven months.

5) Its fate is unknown: traditions say it went to Babylon, was hidden by King Josiah, or was concealed by Jeremiah in a cave on Mount Nebo, while the Ethiopian Orthodox Church says it rests in Axum, and no verified evidence confirms any of them.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ark_of_the_Covenant
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Ark of the Covenant?

Answer: B) Dingonek

The dingonek is a creature said to have been seen near Lake Victoria in 1907 by big game hunter John Alfred Jordan and his party, as told in Edgar Beecher Bronson's 1910 memoir In Closed Territory. Jordan described a beast fourteen or fifteen feet long lying in the Maggori River, with a head as big as a lioness's but marked like a leopard, two long white fangs hanging from its upper jaw, a back as broad as a hippo's and scaled like an armadillo, and a broad fin tail. He fired a .303 rifle behind its ear, it sprang out of the water, and he ran into the bush, and he never saw it again.

How'd you do?

posts.text:
Flathead Lake, northwestern Montana. First reported in 1889.

The story begins long before the steamboats. In a Kutenai legend, two girls crossing the frozen lake one winter see antlers about two feet long sticking up through the ice. When they cut at the ice with sharp-edged rocks to take them, the antlers start to shake, the frozen surface splits open, and the head of a monster rises through it. The legend says half of the tribe drowned in the lake.

According to retired newspaper editor Paul Fugleberg, the first report supposedly comes in 1889 from Captain James C. Kerr of the lake steamboat U.S. Grant. Kerr says he and his 100 passengers saw an unusually large whale-like object in the water, and one of the passengers shot at it and sent it diving.

Locals named it Flessie, after Nessie. Sightings average one or two a year, and in 1993 alone there were about thirteen reports. Witnesses describe a large, round, eel-shaped creature twenty to forty feet long with a wavy, snakelike body, brownish to bluish-black skin, and grayish-black eyes, often compared to a whale or a giant sturgeon. In the 1950s a cash reward was offered for the lake's superfish, and a seven-and-a-half-foot sturgeon weighing just over 181 pounds is now displayed at the Polson-Flathead Historical Museum. Whether that settles it is up to you.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flathead_Lake_Monster

posts.text:
Louisville, Kentucky. Waverly Hills Sanatorium, opened in 1910.

In the early 1900s tuberculosis, known as the White Plague, is ravaging Jefferson County, and Louisville has one of the highest TB death rates in the United States. Waverly Hills opens as a two-story wooden hospital for forty to fifty patients. On October 17, 1926, a massive five-story building opens on the hill, made to hold more than four hundred.

Patients spend their treatments outdoors on long porches. A five-hundred-foot tunnel runs between the heating plant at the bottom of the hill and the main building, with a cable car to carry steam and supplies. According to a number of stories, for a time between the 1920s and 1940s the tunnel also carried something else: corpses, moved discreetly down to a waiting ambulance so the patients would not know someone had died.

The antibiotic streptomycin shrinks the need for the place, and the sanatorium closes in June 1961. It reopens as Woodhaven Geriatric Center, which closes in 1980 after reports of overcrowding and neglect. Plans for a prison, apartments, and even the world's tallest statue of Jesus on the roof all fall through. Today tours run inside the building, it is marketed as a haunted hospital, and Ghost Hunters, Ghost Adventures, and BuzzFeed Unsolved have all come to film there.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waverly_Hills_Sanatorium
posts.headline: Louisville, Kentucky. Waverly Hills Sanatorium, opened in 1910.

posts.text:
Santa Fe, New Mexico. The Loretto Chapel, sometime between 1877 and 1881.

The Sisters of Loretto have a beautiful Gothic Revival chapel for their girls' school, modeled on the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, built of local sandstone and consecrated in 1878. There is one problem. There is no way up to the choir loft. According to the sisters, builder after builder is consulted, and none can find a workable solution in the cramped space.

So the sisters pray to Saint Joseph, the patron saint of carpenters, for nine straight days. On the last day of the novena, a mysterious stranger appears and offers to build a staircase. He works alone with only a few simple hand tools, and when he is done he disappears without collecting his pay. The sisters never learn who he is.

What he leaves behind is a helix of wood that rises twenty feet to the loft and makes two full turns with no central pole, held together with wooden pegs instead of nails. There are thirty-three steps, the age of Christ at his death. Without railings it was so frightening to descend that some nuns and students went down on their hands and knees. The sisters believed the carpenter was Saint Joseph himself.

In the early 2000s, amateur historian Mary Jean Cook pointed to François-Jean "Frenchy" Rochas, a reclusive French rancher and occasional carpenter, as the probable builder, though others dispute it. Either way, the Miraculous Stair became one of Santa Fe's most famous tourist attractions.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loretto_Chapel
posts.headline: Santa Fe, New Mexico. The Loretto Chapel, sometime between 1877 and 1881.

Ste. Genevieve, Missouri. About 9:35 p.m. on October 6, 2026.

Two witnesses, both listed as law enforcement, are watching the north to northeast sky over Ste. Genevieve when they realize they are looking at roughly ten illuminated objects at once. The lights are bright white and sit about 45 degrees above the horizon.

They are not moving together. Each object moves independently of the others, with rapid changes in direction and apparent altitude, sudden acceleration, and illumination that comes and goes. The witnesses say the objects become significantly brighter just before they turn difficult or impossible to see, and then they reappear. The title on the report says it best: lights dogfighting over Ste. Genevieve.

The display lasts about thirty minutes. Aircraft are noted in the area, but the two witnesses are unable to positively identify the objects as aircraft, drones, satellites, or any other known aerial phenomenon. The report is posted to the National UFO Reporting Center on October 13, and so far there is no NUFORC explanation attached to it.

Source: https://nuforc.org/sighting/?id=201453

posts.text:
Monroe County, Ohio. About 5:30 in the morning, in an account published September 26, 2026.

A coal miner is driving home from the night shift in southeastern Ohio when he notices something large crouched in the road ahead of him. It has bright, glowing red eyes, and they look directly at him. Very large wings are wrapped around its body as it crouches there. He has never seen anything like it in his life.

He drives past it. When he looks behind him, it is simply gone. He never saw it take off or leave.

His son hears the story on a phone call. His father tells him it happened the previous week, and his voice is shaky in a way the son has never heard before. The father is normally a skeptic, and he will not even say which road it was, because he believes his son would go out and investigate. He had never heard the name Mothman. People who heard his story gave it that name afterward.

The son sent the account to Phantoms & Monsters, which notes there is no exact date, no named witness, no exact location, and no image, and that an animal misidentification or a misleading visual impression is still possible. The son writes that he hopes the old idea about these sightings bringing bad luck isn't true. Still, a miner says that one morning around 5:30, something with red eyes looked straight at him from the road.

Source: https://deadofnightdispatch.com/dispatches/monroe-county-ohio-mothman-coal-miner-red-eyes-road/

Have you heard of the Voynich manuscript?

Top 5 things to know about the unreadable book:

1) The Voynich manuscript is an illustrated codex written in an undeciphered script nicknamed Voynichese, with fantastical plants, bathing figures, and astrological diagrams on most pages.

2) University of Arizona radiocarbon dating of the calfskin parchment puts it between 1404 and 1438, and stylistic clues point toward an Italian Renaissance origin even though the text remains unread.

3) It is named for Polish book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, who bought it in 1912; the first confirmed earlier owner was Prague alchemist Georg Baresch in the seventeenth century.

4) American and British codebreakers including William and Elizebeth Friedman studied it without success, and no proposed decipherment has been independently verified.

5) Since 1969 it has lived at Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, which published the entire manuscript online in 2020, keeping the world's most famous unread book in public view.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voynich_manuscript
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Voynich manuscript?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Nazca lines?

Top 5 things to know about Peru's desert geoglyphs:

1) The Nazca lines are geoglyphs etched into the Nazca Desert of southern Peru between about 500 BC and 500 AD by removing reddish pebbles to expose lighter soil underneath.

2) Most are straight lines and geometric shapes, but more than seventy are animals and plants, including a hummingbird, monkey, spider, condor, and a human figure, some hundreds of meters long.

3) Together the lines run more than 1,300 kilometers and cover about fifty square kilometers on the dry, windless plateau between Nazca and Palpa, which is why so many have survived.

4) Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejia Xesspe spotted them while hiking in 1927, and American historian Paul Kosok, flying over in 1940 to 1941, realized one design was a bird and linked others to solstice alignments.

5) Scholars generally give them religious meaning rather than landing-strip fantasies, and UNESCO named the lines a World Heritage Site in 1994; drones keep finding hundreds of new figures.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_lines
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Nazca lines?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the dybbuk?

Top 5 things to know about Judaism's clinging spirit:

1) In Jewish mythology a dybbuk is a malicious possessing spirit understood as the dislocated soul of a dead person, from the Hebrew root meaning to adhere or cling.

2) The term appears in sixteenth-century writings and was popularized for wider audiences by S. An-sky's 1920 Yiddish play The Dybbuk, later filmed in 1937 as a classic of Yiddish cinema.

3) Early modern accounts cluster in kabbalistic Safed and Ottoman Galilee, where doctrines of gilgul, the transmigration of souls, gave rabbis a framework for why a restless dead soul might enter the living.

4) Traditionally the spirit was said to leave once it finished its task or was exorcised, and possession narratives often involved confession, unfinished guilt, or family conflict as much as supernatural terror.

5) Modern cases still surface and remain contested, including a widely televised 1999 exorcism in Dimona, Israel, while other rabbinic voices insist many claims belong to psychiatry rather than ritual.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dybbuk
posts.headline: Have you heard of the dybbuk?

posts.text:
Have you heard of crop circles?

Top 5 things to know about the flattened-field mystery:

1) A crop circle is a pattern made by flattening cereal crops, usually wheat or barley, and the term itself was coined in the early 1980s as reports surged in southern England.

2) Fringe theories have blamed aliens or obscure natural forces, but physicists note that published circles fall within the range of human hoaxing, and no scientific evidence supports exotic causes.

3) In 1991, Doug Bower and Dave Chorley publicly took credit for making more than two hundred English crop circles with planks, rope, and a baseball cap fitted with a loop of wire as a sight.

4) After their interviews, the number of reported formations jumped, and circles in Britain tend to appear near roads and areas of medium to high population rather than randomly across remote land.

5) Earlier odd flattened patches exist in the record, including the 1966 Tully "saucer nest" in Australia, but the classic pictogram boom is a late-twentieth-century media and hoax phenomenon.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_circle
posts.headline: Have you heard of crop circles?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the foo fighters?

Top 5 things to know about the WWII mystery lights:

1) Allied night-fighter pilots in World War II used "foo fighters" for unidentified glowing objects that paced their aircraft over Europe and the Pacific, with formal reports clustering from November 1944 onward.

2) The name stuck after radar operator Donald J. Meiers of the U.S. 415th Night Fighter Squadron borrowed "foo" from the Smokey Stover comic strip during a November 27, 1944 debriefing at their base near Dijon, France.

3) Crews described fiery balls of red, white, or orange light that made wild turns, flew in formation with planes, and vanished, yet never opened fire, leading many to assume a secret enemy weapon.

4) Similar sightings were later acknowledged among German and Japanese pilots as well, undercutting the simple idea that only one side was testing a new device.

5) After the war the Robertson Panel floated explanations such as St. Elmo's fire, electromagnetic effects, or light reflecting from ice crystals, but the wartime reports remain a foundational chapter of modern UFO lore.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_fighter
posts.headline: Have you heard of the foo fighters?

Answer: D) Inkanyamba

The Inkanyamba is a legendary serpent of South African Zulu and Xhosa folklore, said to dwell especially in the deep pool at Howick Falls on the Umgeni River in KwaZulu-Natal, where locals nickname it Howie. Tellings cast it as a huge serpentine dragon or storm spirit whose coiling body can stretch from water to sky, often with a horse-like or dragon-like head, sometimes fins, wings, or horns. Summer storms and tornadoes are blamed on its anger, and contact is said to be deadly.

posts.text:
East of Marfa, Texas, on the high Chihuahuan Desert. First written account in 1883.

Young cowhand Robert Reed Ellison is driving cattle through Paisano Pass when he sees a flickering light and wonders if it is an Apache campfire. Other settlers say they have seen the same lights and found no ashes when they rode out. Joe and Anne Humphreys report them again in 1885. The first magazine write-up lands in Coronet in July 1957.

Modern skywatchers gather at a roadside viewing area about nine miles east of town on U.S. 90, looking south-southwest toward Chinati Peak and Mitchell Flat. Witnesses describe orbs that change intensity and color, usually yellow-orange but sometimes green, blue, or red, hovering above desert scrub, splitting, merging, or drifting where ranch lights do not belong.

A University of Texas at Dallas student team in May 2004 timed lights against traffic on Highway 67 and concluded the ones they recorded were car headlights distorted by desert air. Other researchers still log unexplained nights. The lights remain Marfa's signature mystery, half tourist draw and half unanswered desert file.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marfa_lights
posts.headline: East of Marfa, Texas, on the high Chihuahuan Desert. First written account in 1883.

posts.text:
Hill of Tepeyac, outside what is now Mexico City. December 1531.

According to the Nican Mopohua, Juan Diego, a Chichimec peasant, sees a young woman on Tepeyac who speaks Nahuatl and identifies herself as Mary, mother of the true deity. She asks for a church on that hill. Archbishop Juan de Zumárraga does not believe him and demands a miraculous sign.

On December 12, after the Virgin intercepts Juan Diego on his way to find a priest for his dying uncle, she tells him to gather flowers from the barren, freezing summit. He finds Castile roses, not native to Mexico, blooming there. She arranges them in his tilma. When he opens the cloak before Zumárraga, the roses fall and an image of the Virgin appears on the fabric.

The next day his uncle Juan Bernardino is well and says he also saw her, and that she wished to be known as Guadalupe. The tilma is installed in a chapel on Tepeyac by December 26. Today it hangs in the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, the most-visited Catholic shrine in the world.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Lady_of_Guadalupe
posts.headline: Hill of Tepeyac, outside what is now Mexico City. December 1531.

posts.text:
St. Francisville, Louisiana. The Myrtles Plantation, built in 1796.

The antebellum house sits behind a 125-foot veranda of ornamental cast iron and is now a bed and breakfast famous for ghost tourism. In 1948 Clarence John Laughlin noted its haunted presence in Ghosts Along the Mississippi. By the 1980s the National Enquirer had dubbed it America's Most Haunted House, and guidebooks still give it more entries than almost any other plantation.

The only verified murder in the house is that of William Drew Winter, shot on the front porch. Legend says he staggered or crawled up the main staircase and collapsed on the seventeenth step, and visitors still report a presence that stops there. A mirror in the house is said to hold the spirits of Sara Woodruff and two of her children, overlooked when mirrors should have been covered after a death, with handprints sometimes claimed on the glass.

The most told story is of Chloe, an enslaved woman in a green turban who supposedly poisoned a birthday cake with oleander. Historians note there is no record of a slave named Chloe, and Sara and her children died of yellow fever, not poison. Still, the Mystery Tours run nightly, and the house has been filmed for Unsolved Mysteries, Ghost Hunters, Ghost Adventures, and a 2024 Netflix Files of the Unexplained episode.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtles_Plantation
posts.headline: St. Francisville, Louisiana. The Myrtles Plantation, built in 1796.

posts.text:
Burke, Fairfax County, Virginia. October 1970.

On the night of October 19, U.S. Air Force Academy cadet Robert Bennett and his fiancée are parked in a field on Guinea Road when something moves outside the rear window. A man in a white suit with long bunny ears runs from the bushes, shouts that they are on private property, and throws a hatchet through the passenger window. They flee uninjured. The hatchet is still on the floorboard when police arrive. His fiancée remembers a white hood more than ears, but both say they saw his face clearly in the dark.

Ten days later, on Halloween night, construction security guard Paul Phillips finds a man in a gray, black, and white bunny costume on the porch of an unfinished house in Kings Park West on Guinea Road. Phillips puts him at about twenty years old, five foot eight, and one hundred seventy-five pounds. When Phillips speaks, the man starts chopping a porch post with a long-handled axe, then warns that trespassers will lose their heads. Phillips goes for his handgun. By the time he returns, the figure has run into the woods.

Fairfax County Public Library historian Brian A. Conley later ties both reports to the Bunny Man legend. Most later versions move the story to Colchester Overpass near Clifton, the Southern Railway span locals call Bunny Man Bridge.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunny_Man
posts.headline: Burke, Fairfax County, Virginia. October 1970.

posts.text:
Chicago O'Hare International Airport. Afternoon of November 7, 2006.

Around 4:15 p.m., a United Airlines ramp worker pushing back Flight 446 for Charlotte looks up and sees a dark gray metallic disc hovering over Gate C-17. He radios the crew. Within minutes, about a dozen United employees, including pilots, managers, and mechanics, are outside watching a silent saucer estimated between six and twenty-four feet across.

No air traffic controllers see it. Radar does not paint it. Several people outside the airport also report a disc over the field. One witness says it shoots straight up through the cloud deck and leaves a clean blue hole that closes behind it. The object is visible for roughly five minutes.

United Airlines and the FAA first say they have nothing. After the Chicago Tribune files a FOIA request, an internal review finds a United supervisor's call to the tower about the UFO. The FAA calls it a weather phenomenon, possibly a hole-punch cloud, and declines to investigate further. Witnesses remain upset that one of the world's busiest airports brushed off a craft hovering in plain sight over an active gate.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_O'Hare_International_Airport_UFO_sighting
posts.headline: Chicago O'Hare International Airport. Afternoon of November 7, 2006.

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Tower of Babel?

Top 5 things to know about the tower that scattered the languages:

1) The Tower of Babel story in Genesis 11 is an origin myth meant to explain why the world has many languages and cultures, though the Bible itself never uses the exact phrase "Tower of Babel."

2) In the account, a united human race speaking one language settles in Shinar, Lower Mesopotamia, and sets out to build a city and a tower that will reach the sky.

3) Yahweh sees their unity and power, confounds their speech so they can no longer understand one another, and scatters them across the earth, leaving the city unfinished.

4) The Hebrew name Babel is linked in the story to the verb balal, "to jumble or confuse," a wordplay on the name of Babylon, whose Akkadian name Bab-ilim meant "gate of God."

5) Modern scholars often connect the tale to real Mesopotamian ziggurats, especially Etemenanki, the great temple tower of Marduk in Babylon, and a related confusion-of-tongues theme appears in the older Sumerian story Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_Babel
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Tower of Babel?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Mary Celeste?

Top 5 things to know about the most famous ghost ship:

1) Mary Celeste was a Canadian-built, American-registered merchant brigantine found adrift and deserted in the Atlantic Ocean off the Azores on December 4, 1872, by the brigantine Dei Gratia.

2) The ship was in a dishevelled but seaworthy condition under partial sail, with its lifeboat missing, and the last log entry was dated ten days earlier.

3) She had left New York City for Genoa on November 7 with a cargo of alcohol that was still intact when found, and the captain's and crew's personal belongings were undisturbed.

4) None of the people who had been on board were ever seen or heard from again, and the salvage hearings that followed in Gibraltar only deepened the mystery.

5) Built in Spencers Island, Nova Scotia, and launched in 1861 as Amazon before being renamed under American ownership in 1868, Mary Celeste had sailed uneventfully until that 1872 voyage that made her name a byword for unexplained disappearance.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Celeste
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Mary Celeste?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Cottingley Fairies?

Top 5 things to know about the fairy photographs that fooled a nation:

1) The Cottingley Fairies appear in five photographs taken in 1917 by cousins Elsie Wright, then 16, and Frances Griffiths, then 9, beside a beck behind the family house in Cottingley, near Bradford, England.

2) The first plate showed Frances behind a bush with four fairies dancing in front of her, and a later shot showed Elsie on the lawn holding out her hand to a gnome about a foot tall.

3) Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes, used the pictures to illustrate a fairy article in the Christmas 1920 Strand Magazine and treated them as clear evidence of the supernatural.

4) Elsie's father, an amateur photographer, dismissed the figures as cardboard cutouts from the start, but public fascination lasted for decades after interest first faded in the early 1920s.

5) In the early 1980s both women admitted the photographs were faked with cardboard cutouts copied from a children's book, though Frances still maintained that the fifth and final photograph was genuine, and the photos and cameras are now held by the National Science and Media Museum in Bradford.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottingley_Fairies
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Cottingley Fairies?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Battle of Los Angeles?

Top 5 things to know about the Great Los Angeles Air Raid of 1942:

1) The Battle of Los Angeles is the name newspapers gave to a rumored Japanese air attack and the anti-aircraft barrage that lit up the sky over Los Angeles from late February 24 into early February 25, 1942.

2) It came less than three months after Pearl Harbor and one day after a Japanese submarine shelled Ellwood near Santa Barbara, when West Coast cities were already running blackouts and bracing for invasion.

3) Gunners poured anti-aircraft fire into the night. Five civilians died during the barrage, and four Japanese aircraft were erroneously reported shot down, though no enemy planes were ever confirmed.

4) Secretary of the Navy Frank Knox called the episode a "false alarm" soon afterward, while some newspapers speculated about a cover-up to hide a real raid.

5) Later official histories pointed to a meteorological balloon sent aloft around 1:00 am as the trigger, with war nerves, stray flares and shell bursts from neighboring batteries feeding the chaos, and the U.S. Office of Air Force History in 1983 summed it up as war nerves sparked by a lost weather balloon.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Los_Angeles
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Battle of Los Angeles?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Shroud of Turin?

Top 5 things to know about the cloth some believe wrapped Jesus:

1) The Shroud of Turin is a length of linen bearing a faint image of the front and back of a naked man, with details that match traditional depictions of Jesus after crucifixion, and it has been venerated for centuries especially in the Catholic Church.

2) The image is clearer in photographic negative, a fact that drew worldwide attention after Secondo Pia photographed the shroud in 1898 and saw a lifelike positive face appear on his negative plate.

3) In 1988, radiocarbon dating by three independent laboratories dated samples of the cloth to the Middle Ages, between 1260 and 1390, a result most experts accept even as public debate continues.

4) Forensic microscopist Walter McCrone, examining adhesive-tape samples taken in 1978, argued the image was painted with red ochre in a gelatin medium and that the apparent bloodstains were vermilion pigment, findings other researchers dispute.

5) Defenders of authenticity often argue the tested samples were contaminated or taken from a medieval repair, but those fringe theories have been rejected by most experts, and the nature of the image remains contested in both scholarly literature and the popular press.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shroud_of_Turin
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Shroud of Turin?

posts.text:
Answer: C) Squonk

The squonk is a mythical creature said to live in the hemlock forests of northern Pennsylvania. The earliest written account appears in the 1910 book Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, which describes a shy, always-unhappy animal with loose warty skin that weeps constantly, leaving a tear-stained trail hunters can follow. When cornered or badly frightened, the story goes, it may dissolve itself entirely in its own tears. Its mock scientific name, Lacrimacorpus dissolvens, is Latin for a body that dissolves in tears, and Johnstown, Pennsylvania, still celebrates it each August at Squonkapalooza.

How'd you do?

posts.text:
Fatima, Portugal. October 13, 1917.

Tens of thousands of people crowd the Cova da Iria after three shepherd children, Lucia Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, say the Virgin Mary promised a miracle on this date so that all may believe. It has been raining. The ground is mud.

Then, according to scores of witnesses, the clouds break. The Sun appears as an opaque, spinning disc, duller than usual, throwing multicolored light across the landscape, the crowd and the clouds. Many say it careens toward the Earth before zig-zagging back into place. The event lasts about ten minutes. Some report that their soaked clothes and the muddy ground dry suddenly. Not everyone sees the same thing. Some see only the colors. Some see the Lady. Some see nothing at all. Crowd estimates run from about 50,000 to about 70,000.

Secular reporters and officials are among those who describe the solar display. The local bishop opens a canonical investigation that November, and on October 13, 1930, Bishop Jose da Silva declares the miracle worthy of belief. Critics later argue the accounts are inconsistent and that staring at the Sun can trick the eyes. Believers still call it the Miracle of the Sun.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracle_of_the_Sun
posts.headline: Fatima, Portugal. October 13, 1917.

posts.text:
Darien, Georgia, near the mouth of the Altamaha River. 1981.

Former newspaper publisher Larry Gwin is fishing with his friend Steven Wilson in the coastal marshes when something big moves in the water. They say it shows two humps about five feet apart and leaves a wake like a speedboat. Newspapers across the country pick up the story, and other witnesses start talking.

Harvey Blackman of Brunswick says he saw it in the 1970s at a spot called Two Way on the Altamaha, a snake-like head on a body fifteen to twenty feet long. Frank Culpepper reports a wake so large it bounced the boats, and one of his companions ran for a rifle before the thing was gone. Believers describe an animal up to about thirty feet long with flippers like a seal.

People have been telling versions of this for a long time. In April 1830, Captain Delano of the schooner Eagle reported a creature about seventy feet long off St. Simons Island, alligator-shaped head raised about eight feet out of the water, and other men on the schooner backed him up. Darien itself was founded by Scottish Highlanders from the Inverness country around Loch Ness. Locals just call the modern beast the Altamaha-ha, or Altie.

Source: https://www.exploresouthernhistory.com/altamahaha.html
posts.headline: Darien, Georgia, near the mouth of the Altamaha River. 1981.

posts.text:
San Jose, California. 1886 to 1922.

Sarah Winchester, widow of the Winchester rifle fortune, buys a two-story farmhouse on forty-five acres near San Jose and starts expanding it herself. Room by room. Stairways that rise only a few feet. Doors and windows that end up sealed inside new walls. A seven-story tower torn down and rebuilt again and again. By the time she dies on September 7, 1922, the place is a maze.

Nine months later it opens as a tourist attraction. The stories grow with the house. A popular telling, traced by historians to a 1967 book, says Sarah visited a Boston medium who told her the ghosts of people killed by Winchester rifles were on her, and that she must build a house for them and never finish it. Researchers have found no solid evidence she met that medium, but the legend stuck to the brochures.

Today visitors and guides still report cold spots, footsteps, cooking smells, whispering, doors slamming on their own, and the feeling of being watched. Skeptic Joe Nickell chalks it up to suggestion and a drafty Victorian labyrinth. Believers call it one of America's most haunted houses. Either way, the halls keep turning, and the doors still lead nowhere.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_Mystery_House
posts.headline: San Jose, California. 1886 to 1922.

posts.text:
Colorado. October 1, 2023.

A local law enforcement officer in Colorado looks up and starts filming. What he sees, he later calls an orb. Silent. Red, blue and green lights flashing. He puts it at about 300 feet off the ground. A radar check, he says, shows no aircraft in the area.

According to a redacted transcript later released with the case, the object hangs there for about fifteen minutes, then starts to fly closer. The exact town name is blacked out in the public file.

On September 18, 2026, the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office publishes the material as PURSUE Release 06: four cellphone clips from that same night, plus the one-page transcript. Parts of the videos are blurred at the bottom to protect privacy. Officials note the footage came from a cellular device, and that autofocus and image processing can distort distant subjects.

AARO has not identified the object. The case remains unresolved. No claim of exotic technology appears in the official record. Just a silent, multicolored orb on a Colorado night, recorded by a cop, and still unexplained years later.

Source: https://www.denvergazette.com/2026/09/22/feds-share-video-of-uap-that-was-captured-by-law-enforcement-in-colorado/
posts.headline: Colorado. October 1, 2023.

posts.text:
Near Winona, Minnesota. Late 1960s.

In a refrigerated glass coffin on a private property near Winona, carnival promoter Frank Hansen is touring something he bills as the missing link. Inside the ice is a hairy, manlike figure about six feet tall, with large hands and feet, dark brown hair three to four inches long, and a flattened nose. One arm looks broken. One eye looks knocked from its socket, as if by a bullet from behind.

Hansen tells audiences it was found in Siberia and that he is only the caretaker for an eccentric California millionaire. Canada Customs once detains him on suspicion he is hauling a human cadaver. The FBI is told it might be a murder victim, but no investigation follows.

In April 1969, Argosy science editor Ivan T. Sanderson puts the Iceman on the magazine cover and asks whether this is the missing link between man and the apes. He contacts Smithsonian primatologist John Napier. Hansen then pulls the exhibit, saying the California owner ordered it withdrawn, and later puts a new Iceman on the road that observers call an obvious latex model.

Napier concludes Hansen had commissioned a West Coast company to make the figure in 1967, and that the original and the so-called substitute were the same carnival prop, repositioned and refrozen between shows. The Smithsonian is satisfied it is latex rubber and hair. In 2013 the sideshow gaff sells on eBay and ends up on display at the Museum of the Weird in Austin, Texas.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Iceman
posts.headline: Near Winona, Minnesota. Late 1960s.

posts.text:
Have you heard of Tartarus?

Top 5 things to know about the abyss where the fallen angels are chained:

1) In Greek mythology, Tartarus is the deep abyss used as a dungeon of torment for the wicked and as the prison of the Titans, and in Hesiod's Theogony it is one of the earliest beings to exist, alongside Chaos and Gaia.

2) In the Iliad, Zeus says Tartarus is "as far beneath Hades as heaven is above earth," and Hesiod says a bronze anvil falling from heaven would take nine days to reach earth and nine more to reach Tartarus.

3) Its prisoners included the Titans after they lost to the gods of Olympus, plus the Cyclopes and the hundred-armed Hecatonchires, and later myths filled it with mortals like Sisyphus, Tantalus and Ixion, each given a punishment to fit his crime.

4) In the Greek text of the Book of Enoch, dated to 400 to 200 BC, God places the archangel Uriel "in charge of the world and of Tartarus," generally understood as the place where 200 fallen Watchers are imprisoned.

5) The New Testament never uses the noun, but 2 Peter 2:4 uses a verb meaning "throw to Tartarus," saying God did not spare angels when they sinned but "cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment," and Jude 1:6 describes angels bound in chains under everlasting darkness.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartarus
posts.headline: Have you heard of Tartarus?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Bermuda Triangle?

Top 5 things to know about the Devil's Triangle:

1) The Bermuda Triangle, also called the Devil's Triangle, is a loosely defined region of the North Atlantic roughly bounded by Florida, Bermuda and Puerto Rico, and the urban legend that ships and planes vanish there under mysterious circumstances dates only from the mid-20th century.

2) The earliest suggestion of unusual disappearances near Bermuda appeared in an article by Edward Van Winkle Jones of the Miami Herald, distributed by the Associated Press on September 17, 1950, and in 1952 Fate magazine's "Sea Mystery at Our Back Door" first laid out the now-familiar triangle.

3) The legend's centerpiece is Flight 19, five US Navy torpedo bombers lost on a training mission in December 1945, and a 1962 magazine article claimed the flight leader said, "We cannot be sure of any direction ... everything is wrong ... strange ... the ocean doesn't look as it should."

4) Vincent Gaddis popularized the idea in a 1964 Argosy article called "The Deadly Bermuda Triangle," later writers including Charles Berlitz in 1974 added supernatural elements, and they couldn't even agree on the boundaries, which ranged from 1.3 to 3.9 million square kilometers.

5) Researcher Larry Kusche's 1975 book The Bermuda Triangle Mystery: Solved concluded that the number of ships and aircraft lost there was not significantly greater than in any other part of the ocean, and Lloyd's of London and the US Coast Guard found no evidence of unusual activity either.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda_Triangle
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Bermuda Triangle?

posts.text:
Have you heard of the Golem?

Top 5 things to know about the clay giant of Jewish folklore:

1) A golem is an animated humanlike being in Jewish folklore made entirely from inanimate matter, usually clay or mud, and the word appears just once in the Bible, in Psalm 139, for the unfinished human being before God's eyes.

2) The Talmud says Adam himself was first a golem when his dust was kneaded into a shapeless husk, and the earliest known written account of how to create one comes from Eleazar of Worms in the late 12th and early 13th centuries.

3) In the tales, a golem is brought to life by writing the name of God on a slip of paper placed in its mouth or forehead, or by writing the Hebrew word emet, "truth," on its forehead, and erasing the first letter turns it into met, "dead."

4) The most famous golem is the one Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague supposedly made in the late 16th century from clay on the banks of the Vltava River to defend the Prague ghetto, called Josef or Yossele, whom he deactivated each Friday evening so it could rest on the Sabbath.

5) Legend says its body still lies in the attic of Prague's Old New Synagogue, though when the attic was renovated in 1883 no evidence of it was found, and historians generally view the Prague story as a German literary invention of the early 19th century.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golem
posts.headline: Have you heard of the Golem?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Area 51?

Top 5 things to know about the secret Nevada air base:

1) Area 51 is a highly classified US Air Force facility in southern Nevada, 83 miles north-northwest of Las Vegas, officially called Homey Airport or Groom Lake after the salt flat beside its airfield.

2) The CIA established the Groom Lake test site in April 1955 for Project AQUATONE, the Lockheed U-2 spy plane, and designer Kelly Johnson said that flying over it, "within thirty seconds, you knew that was the place."

3) The Air Force officially acknowledged the site's existence in 1998, and on June 25, 2013 the CIA released a history confirming the U-2 was tested there, in response to a Freedom of Information Act request filed in 2005.

4) Its UFO reputation partly came from its own aircraft, since the U-2 flew above 60,000 feet and airline pilots saw its silver wings catch the setting sun, and OXCART veterans said airline pilots cruising over Nevada at dusk would see the spy plane whiz by at 2,000-plus mph and think UFO, so Project Blue Book checked flight records to dismiss most of those reports.

5) Bob Lazar claimed in 1989 that he worked on alien spacecraft at an underground site called S-4 near Papoose Lake, and in July 2019 more than 2,000,000 people responded to a joke Facebook post to "Storm Area 51," though only between 1,500 and 3,000 people showed up at two nearby festivals and seven people were reportedly arrested.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_51
posts.headline: Have you heard of Area 51?

posts.text:
Have you heard of Sodom and Gomorrah?

Top 5 things to know about the cities of the plain destroyed in Genesis:

1) Sodom and Gomorrah were two of the "cities of the plain" in the story of Abraham and Lot, destroyed by God for their wickedness in Genesis 19:1-28, and the story parallels the Genesis flood narrative in its theme of God's anger at human sin.

2) Before the destruction, Abraham bargains with God, asking "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" and starting at 50 people, he gets God to agree to spare Sodom if ten righteous people can be found.

3) Two angels are welcomed into Lot's home and lead him, his wife and his two daughters out of the city, then God rains sulfur and fire on the plain, and Lot's wife, who ignores the warning and looks back, is turned into a pillar of salt.

4) Ezekiel 16:49-50 describes the iniquity of Sodom as "pride, fulness of bread, and careless ease" while the poor and needy went unhelped, and Deuteronomy, Isaiah and Jeremiah use the two cities as a byword for destruction and desolation.

5) The cities may have been based on real places along the Dead Sea, with sites like Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira suggested, and Strabo and Josephus both place Sodom near the Dead Sea, but the archaeological evidence is inconclusive.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodom_and_Gomorrah
posts.headline: Have you heard of Sodom and Gomorrah?
